Peleg
pē'leg
n. (son of Eber, in whose days the earth was divided; the name marks the generation of Babel)
From Hebrew Peleg, division, from palag, to split or divide. Moses supplies the meaning himself in the same breath as the name — the only son in the list whose naming is explained.

Biblical Definition

Peleg is the son of Eber and the brother of Joktan, and he is the one name in the post-flood genealogy that Moses pauses to explain: “And unto Eber were born two sons: the name of one was Peleg; for in his days was the earth divided” (Gen 10:25). The Chronicler repeats the note (1Ch 1:19), which means it was thought worth preserving through the exile and back. The division intended is almost certainly the scattering at Babel, recorded in the very next chapter: men of one language and one speech built a tower to make themselves a name, and “the LORD scattered them abroad from thence upon the face of all the earth: and they left off to build the city” (Gen 11:8). Genesis 10 lists the nations; Genesis 11 explains how they came to be nations. Peleg stands at the hinge. His own line is the plain one — he lived thirty years and begat Reu (Gen 11:18), and through Reu, Serug, Nahor and Terah the promise runs to Abram, so that the man named for the world's fracture is also the man through whom its healing is descended. That is the shape of the whole Bible in a single name: division comes by human pride, and the remedy comes by divine election running quietly through the same family in the same generation.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Peleg; in sacred history he is the son of Eber, so named because in his days the earth was divided.

expand to see more

PELEG, n. The son of Eber and brother of Joktan, whose name signifies division.

He was so called because in his days the earth was divided among the nations.

He lived thirty years and begat Reu, and is an ancestor of Abraham.

The division intended is commonly understood of the dispersion at Babel.

His name is the only one in the post-diluvian genealogy whose reason is given in the text.

Key Scripture

Gen 11:16 — "And Eber lived four and thirty years, and begat Peleg:"

Gen 11:18 — "And Peleg lived thirty years, and begat Reu:"

Gen 11:1 — "And the whole earth was of one language, and of one speech."

Gen 11:8 — "So the LORD scattered them abroad from thence upon the face of all the earth: and they left off to build the city."

Modern Corruption

The division in Peleg's days is regularly reassigned to continental drift or geological catastrophe, which makes a theological judgment into a physics event and loses the point Moses is making.

expand to see more

A popular reading takes “the earth was divided” as the splitting of the continents, and builds a rapid post-flood plate tectonics upon it. The dictionary does not follow. The Hebrew 'erets in this context regularly means the inhabited land and its peoples, and the immediately following chapter supplies the division Moses means without any need to look elsewhere: one speech became many, and the builders were scattered abroad upon the face of all the earth. Genesis 10 has already used the same frame three times over — the sons of Japheth, of Ham, of Shem, each “after their tongues, in their lands, after their nations” (Gen 10:31). The division is linguistic, national, and moral, and it is a judgment. Making it geological trades a doctrine for a mechanism.

The second corruption goes the other way, treating Babel as a myth explaining language diversity — a folk etiology of the kind found in every ancient culture. But Babel is not offered as an explanation of a curiosity; it is offered as an act of God against a specific human project, the attempt to build a name and a unity independent of Him. That project did not end in Shinar. Every generation rebuilds the tower under a new name, and Scripture's answer to it is not the abolition of nations but their conversion — the scattering at Babel answered at Pentecost, where the tongues are not merged but every man hears in his own, and answered finally by a multitude out of every kindred and tongue standing before the throne (Rev 7:9).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Peleg (H6389), Peleg, division; palag (H6385), to split, divide; 'erets (H776), earth, land; puts (H6327), to scatter; balal (H1101), to confuse.

expand to see more

Hebrew Peleg (H6389) — Peleg; the name means division and is explained in the text itself.

Hebrew palag (H6385) — to split, cleave, divide; the root from which the name is drawn.

Hebrew 'erets (H776) — earth, land, the inhabited world and its peoples.

Hebrew puts (H6327) — to scatter, disperse; the LORD's act against the builders in Gen 11:8.

Hebrew balal (H1101) — to mingle, confound; the verb behind the name Babel.

Usage

"“In his days was the earth divided” — a name that dates a judgment."

"“The whole earth was of one language, and of one speech” — the unity men lost by grasping at it."

"The generation of the fracture is the generation of the promised line."
